# Futurescape Application Architecture and Developer Standard

**Futurescape Technologies Pvt. Ltd. | Version 1.0 | 29 September 2026**  
**Audience:** new developers, tech leads, QA, DevOps, and architects  
**Status:** required baseline for new products and material new modules

## 1\. Purpose and decision

Every new Futurescape application must join the existing platform instead of creating its own identity, subscription, CMS, UI language, or integration authority. The default stack is oneSSO (Keycloak) for identity, oneSAAS with Lago for commercial lifecycle and entitlements, Kong OSS for API ingress, **Futurescape's existing self-hosted multi-tenant StrapiCMS instance** for managed frontend content, a shared Material Design 3 token and component system, an Nx monorepo for TypeScript/Next.js code, and domain-owned microservices for business behavior. Flutter uses the same design tokens and contracts; it does not have to live in a JavaScript Nx package to satisfy this standard.

This is an **integration standard**, not a requirement that every application run every product locally. An internal-only tool or a product with no marketing/content surface still registers with oneSAAS and oneSSO; its Strapi integration may be marked `not-applicable` with a reason. A service should become a separately deployed microservice when its domain ownership, data, scale, security, or release cadence justifies it. Start with clear modular boundaries and extract only when there is a concrete need.

### Non-negotiable outcomes

1. One account can enter authorized apps through oneSSO, with separate internal and external realm policy as configured.  
2. oneSAAS owns the app catalogue, tenant activation, entitlement decisions, subscription state and provisioning orchestration; Lago executes billing through oneSAAS.  
3. All supported product APIs are reached through Kong. Backend services still validate identity, membership, entitlement, permission and resource tenant scope.  
4. Managed marketing, help, onboarding and editable presentation content comes from the existing shared Strapi instance; live transactions and application records come from domain services. A new app must not deploy its own Strapi instance by default.  
5. Web and Flutter interfaces share approved semantic Material 3 tokens, accessibility rules and product-specific component adaptations.  
6. Contracts and events make cross-product integration explicit; no direct access to another product's database.  
7. GitLab CI blocks an app that bypasses the required platform controls.

## 2\. Authority map

| Concern | System of record | Product responsibility |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Human identity, login, token issuance | oneSSO / Keycloak | OIDC client registration, token validation, account-to-domain identity mapping |
| Organisation and product access orchestration | oneSAAS | Register app manifest, request tenant activation, consume effective entitlement and quota decisions |
| Prices, plans, subscriptions, invoices, usage | Lago through oneSAAS | Emit usage with stable event IDs; show billing status from oneSAAS; never call Lago from browser/mobile |
| API routing and edge policy | Kong OSS plus reviewed platform policy | Publish versioned OpenAPI and route manifest; use gateway base URL |
| Editable frontend content and media | Existing self-hosted multi-tenant Strapi instance | Register explicit tenant/site/environment mapping; use server-side CMS adapter |
| Product-specific transactions and records | Owning domain service | Own database, migrations, authorization, audit and events |
| Workflows across products | Domain owner \+ RabbitMQ/outbox and approved integration orchestration | Publish versioned events; support idempotent consumers and reconciliation |
| Visual foundation | Shared Material 3 design system | Use semantic tokens, accessible components and documented variations |

oneCRM owns leads and opportunities, oneSocial owns social connections and publication, oneHRMS owns employment/payroll records, and so on. Strapi must not become a shadow CRM, billing engine, authentication directory, or operational database. Email addresses and display names are not identity join keys; use stable subject and explicit mapping IDs.

## 3\. Reference topology

![][image1]

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  W["Next.js web / Flutter app<br/>shared design + typed clients"] --> K["Kong OSS<br/>reviewed routes and edge policy"]
  K --> B["Product BFF / domain API"]
  B --> D["Product-owned data"]
  B --> S["oneSAAS<br/>catalogue + entitlement"]
  S --> L["Lago<br/>billing"]
  B --> C["Strapi content adapter<br/>site and tenant scoped"]
  C --> T["Existing self-hosted<br/>multi-tenant StrapiCMS"]
  I["oneSSO / Keycloak"] --> W
  I --> K
  B --> Q["RabbitMQ + outbox<br/>versioned domain events"]
```

The frontend calls Kong-hosted product APIs and its server-side BFF. A server component/BFF may access Strapi through the approved Kong route using server-held credentials. Browser and mobile code must not contain Lago or Strapi administration credentials. No product service reads another service's tables; integrations use versioned REST APIs, events, or an approved connector. If a synchronous flow requires data from another domain, the owner exposes an API and the caller handles timeout and partial failure.

## 4\. Required integration contracts

### 4.1 oneSSO / Keycloak

- Register a client per application and environment through the approved oneSSO process. Use exact redirect and post-logout URIs; keep internal and external realm policies separate. Public web/mobile clients use Authorization Code with PKCE. Confidential server clients keep credentials in the secrets manager.  
- Browser apps should use the approved BFF/session pattern where available. Do not store privileged tokens or a client secret in frontend bundles. Flutter uses platform secure storage and the approved OIDC flow.  
- Validate token signature with current keys, issuer, audience, expiry, not-before and allowed algorithm. Resolve subject to a local domain reference; do not equate `sub` with an employee ID, customer ID, or tenant ID.  
- Effective action authorization is **identity \+ active membership \+ workspace selection \+ product entitlement \+ permission \+ resource scope**. Submitted `tenantId`, `companyId`, `societyId`, `clientId` or `websiteId` is an untrusted selector that must match authorized server-side mappings.  
- Define invitation, role change, suspension, removal, token/session expiration and access revocation paths. A new CRM client record does not automatically grant its contact a login.

### 4.2 oneSAAS / Lago

- Register every new application in the oneSAAS catalogue using a reviewed, versioned GitLab manifest. Registration defines identity, product code, owner, environments, APIs, features, plans, provisioning adapter, health checks and required integrations. **Registration is separate from tenant activation.**  
- A tenant's activation request passes through oneSAAS. oneSAAS maps the billable customer/subscription through its Lago adapter, determines entitlement, provisions product resources and records state. App code must not create Lago plans, customers, subscriptions or invoices directly.  
- Gate feature and quota use by an effective oneSAAS entitlement decision. Handle trial, active, past-due, suspended, cancelled and recovery states according to product policy; do not infer access from a payment success page or webhook arrival alone.  
- Webhook and provisioning work is idempotent, retried with backoff, audited and reconciled against the system of record. Return a clear `pending` state while dependencies are incomplete. Deny access if a mandatory identity, entitlement or product-provisioning check fails. A transient Lago outage must not silently invent an active entitlement.  
- Usage events include product, tenant, feature/meter, event ID, timestamp and measured quantity; deduplicate before billing. Keep Lago API keys on the oneSAAS server side.

### 4.3 Kong and API contracts

- Product APIs publish a reviewed OpenAPI contract with stable `operationId`, auth requirements, request/response/error schema and compatibility policy. Use the companion [API Contract to Client, Gateway, and MCP Architecture](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1JbIXzM08BBKkF8kibflvcqIbTnkdwNCR/view?usp=drivesdk) for generators, decK conversion and CI details.  
- decK may derive base routing from OpenAPI, then platform-owned policy is merged and reviewed. Kong OSS does not include Kong's Enterprise OpenID Connect plugin; a generated `openid-connect` policy must never be deployed to OSS without replacing it with an approved OSS-compatible validation path.  
- Token validation at the edge is a first gate. Every domain API enforces its own object-level access and tenant isolation. Strip/overwrite untrusted identity headers; do not authorize from `X-Tenant-Id` alone.  
- Use a correlation ID and structured error model. All mutation retries require defined idempotency semantics. Do not expose an upstream service directly to avoid Kong.

### 4.4 StrapiCMS for frontend content

- Connect to Futurescape's **existing self-hosted, multi-tenant StrapiCMS instance** for content that authors need to change without a product release: public pages, onboarding copy, help, FAQs, media, approved templates and content-led product navigation. Do not create a product-local Strapi deployment or database. Keep live balances, subscription decisions, personnel records, lead state, permissions and transactions in domain services.  
- The shared CMS/platform team provisions a tenant/site connection and environment mapping for the new application. Record the Strapi tenant identifier, site identifier, permitted content types, locale policy, media scope, token scope, and owning team in the platform registry. Provisioning is idempotent and revocable; content published in one tenant must not be discoverable by another.  
- Model explicit `organisation → client → website → environment → Strapi tenant/site` mappings where those entities apply. Site name, URL, host header or a submitted tenant ID never establishes authority. Staging and production use separate mappings and secrets.  
- Access Strapi through a server-only CMS adapter/BFF via Kong. Request only scoped content; verify both local mapping and Strapi-side tenant authorization. Do not query Strapi's database or expose a full-access API token in the browser. Scope read, draft, media, publish and approval operations independently.  
- Public, non-personalized content may be cached with a site, locale, version and environment key. Identity, selected organisation, entitlement and provisioning responses must not share a public cache. Content failures should fall back to an approved last-known-good version where safe, with a visible operational alert.  
- Strapi admin SSO is a separately licensed feature in current Strapi documentation. Do not claim that an OSS Strapi admin installation automatically integrates with Keycloak; validate licensing and implement an approved editor access approach before launch. Product-user login remains oneSSO even when CMS editor access has a separate arrangement.

### 4.5 Material Design 3 and shared UI system

- Define a versioned semantic token set for primary/secondary/tertiary colors, surfaces, text, error/warning/success, typography, spacing, shape, elevation, motion, focus and breakpoints. Do not copy raw hex values between apps. Include light, dark and high-contrast checks where supported.  
- Web apps use approved shared components in Nx, themed from semantic Material 3 tokens. Existing Shadcn/Radix or other accessible primitives may be adapted with those tokens; do not replace a working product UI wholesale merely to claim Material 3 compliance. Document deviations at component level.  
- Flutter apps use `ThemeData`/`ColorScheme` and appropriate Material 3 widgets, generated from the same token source where practicable. Maintain a parity review for web and mobile rather than assuming identical widget implementations.  
- Provide accessible labels, keyboard traversal, visible focus, minimum target sizes, screen-reader semantics, responsive layouts and reduced-motion behavior. Check color contrast against WCAG 2.2 AA criteria. Use real empty, loading, permission-denied, error and offline states in component previews.

### 4.6 Nx workspace and microservice boundaries

- Next.js/TypeScript apps use the relevant Nx monorepo and preserve existing repository conventions. Suggested layout: `apps/<product>-web`, `apps/<product>-bff`, `libs/platform/auth`, `libs/platform/entitlements`, `libs/platform/api-clients`, `libs/platform/cms`, `libs/design/tokens`, `libs/design/web`, `libs/<domain>/contracts`, `libs/<domain>/feature-*`.  
- Use Nx tags to enforce scope and type boundaries. Product feature libraries depend on platform contracts, not another product's internal feature library. No import from a service's private source directory. A shared library must have a stable owner and public API.  
- The existing self-hosted Strapi stays outside each product's Nx deployment and release cycle and is operated as shared infrastructure. A PHP/Laravel, Java, Python or Serverpod backend can remain in its own repository when that fits its toolchain; Nx does not require putting every runtime in one process or repo. Provide a versioned API package/contract and CI integration instead.  
- Each microservice owns its schema or database boundary, migration and release. Prefer an initially modular service over a fleet of tiny services that share tables or require lockstep deployment. Use RabbitMQ and a transactional outbox for durable cross-service changes, idempotent consumers, dead-letter handling and reconciliation. n8n may orchestrate approved integrations but is not the transaction or authorization authority.

## 5\. Example new-application lifecycle

![][image2]

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Dev as Developer / GitLab
  participant SaaS as oneSAAS
  participant SSO as oneSSO
  participant Bill as Lago adapter
  participant Prod as Product service
  Dev->>SaaS: Submit reviewed app manifest
  SaaS-->>Dev: App registered (no tenant access yet)
  SaaS->>SSO: Configure approved clients and roles
  SaaS->>Bill: Sync plan and customer mapping
  SaaS->>Prod: Activate tenant (idempotency key)
  Prod-->>SaaS: Provisioned / pending / failed
  SaaS-->>Dev: Reconciled health and effective entitlement
```

&nbsp;

The CLI exposes business operations (`validate`, `plan`, `apply`, `status`, `reconcile`) through oneSAAS, with dry-run, audit, idempotency and production approval gates. It must not administer Keycloak, Lago or Kong directly. A production apply identifies the exact commit and manifest hash. Provisioning uses a state machine with retries and compensation where safe; timeouts are reconciled before retrying an operation whose side effect may already have succeeded.

### Illustrative manifest fields

```yaml
apiVersion: futurescape.io/v1
kind: Application
metadata:
  productCode: oneexample
  ownerTeam: example-team
spec:
  oneSso:
    audience: oneexample-api
    realms: [external]
  oneSaas:
    provisioner: oneexample-tenant-v1
    entitlementFeatures: [example.read, example.write]
  gateway:
    openapiArtifact: contracts/openapi/oneexample-v1.yaml
  cms:
    mode: shared-self-hosted-strapi
    purpose: [marketing, help]
  ui:
    designSystem: futurescape-material-3
  environments: [development, staging, production]
```

This is a conceptual example. The existing oneSAAS manifest schema and CLI are authoritative; developers should extend and validate them rather than creating a competing registration format.

## 6\. Required user and service flows

| Flow | Minimum behavior | Failure path |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Sign in | oneSSO authenticates; app selects an authorized organisation/workspace; product API checks effective access | 401 for missing/invalid identity; 403 for valid identity without grant |
| Activate product | oneSAAS checks plan and entitlement, then provisions product tenant and mappings | State remains `pending` or `failed`; idempotent retry and reconciliation; no premature access |
| Display content | BFF resolves approved Strapi site/environment and fetches scoped content | Bounded last-known-good public content where appropriate; alert on stale data |
| Record billable usage | Product emits one stable usage event; oneSAAS adapter forwards/deduplicates to Lago | Outbox/retry; reconcile count and period; no silent drop or duplicate charge |
| Revoke access | Membership, role, entitlement or tenant status changes invalidate effective access | Backend denies new actions even if an old UI still displays a cached control |
| Cross-product action | Caller has mapped identities, tenant context and explicit receiving-side permission | Deny ambiguous or cross-tenant mapping; record audit and retry safely |

## 7\. Security, tenancy and operational requirements

- Maintain separate development, staging and production oneSSO clients/issuers as configured, Kong/oneSAAS endpoints, AWS secret namespaces, Strapi site mappings and data. Never let non-production credentials access production resources.  
- Resolve identity and tenant context server-side. Scope database queries, Redis keys, object storage paths, search indices, vector stores, exports, background jobs and logs by the verified tenant and resource permission.  
- Protect service-to-service traffic with approved credentials and audience scopes; rotate secrets and signing keys. Reject expired, wrong-audience and wrong-issuer tokens; document key refresh and revocation behavior.  
- Emit trace/correlation IDs across Kong, BFF, services, queue and outbound adapters. Measure login failure, entitlement denial, provisioning lag/failure, Strapi failures, webhook lag, billing reconciliation, queue age and API contract drift. Never log access tokens, API keys or sensitive personal data.  
- Define an SLO and rollback plan for each product. Deploy additive API changes before client updates; keep old mobile contract versions supported through the agreed compatibility window.

## 8\. New developer delivery sequence

1. Read the domain ownership map and choose the product/service owner. Write a one-page boundary decision: owned data, APIs, events, tenants, expected scale and why a separate service is or is not needed.  
2. Find the existing Nx workspace and oneSAAS app manifest schema. Add the app/module there; do not start a rival platform shell. Register the product code, owner and environments through the approved oneSAAS workflow.  
3. Define oneSSO client/audience/role mappings and a permission matrix for internal and external users. Test session expiry, revoked membership and cross-tenant access.  
4. Define plans, features, meters, trial policy, quotas and provisioner in oneSAAS. Test pending, failed, suspended and recovery lifecycle states before billing launch.  
5. Design the OpenAPI contract and event schema. Generate typed clients, route baseline and contract tests. Add Kong policies in the platform pipeline; verify OSS plugin compatibility.  
6. Build frontend features from shared Material 3 tokens/components. Request a tenant/site/environment connection on the existing Strapi instance and implement the server-only adapter for editable content; if the product has no such content, record the `not-applicable` CMS decision.  
7. Implement product-owned persistence, outbox, idempotency, observability and domain authorization. Never use another service's database or browser-held platform keys.  
8. Run the release gates in staging, document the runbook and rollback, then use the approved production manifest hash and deployment approval.

### Merge/release gate

| Gate | Evidence required |
| :---- | :---- |
| Platform registration | Reviewed manifest, oneSAAS catalogue record, named owner, separate activation test |
| Identity and access | Keycloak client config, issuer/audience tests, role and membership matrix, denied cross-tenant tests |
| Billing and entitlement | Lago mapping only through oneSAAS, signed webhook validation, idempotent usage, lifecycle reconciliation |
| Gateway and contracts | OpenAPI lint/breaking diff, generated client compile, provider conformance, reviewed decK diff, negative auth tests |
| CMS | Explicit site/environment mapping and Strapi-side isolation; or recorded `not-applicable` decision |
| UI | Token use, responsive keyboard/screen-reader checks, empty/error/loading states and documented deviations |
| Service boundaries | Nx dependency lint, DB ownership, event versioning, outbox/retry tests and no direct upstream bypass |
| Operations | Trace IDs, dashboards, alert ownership, secrets scan, restore/rollback and runbook |

## 9\. Decisions, exceptions and migration

The default is mandatory for **new** work. An exception must name the owner, reason, compensating control, expiration date and migration action, and receive architecture/security review before release. Existing legacy apps move toward this baseline incrementally; do not delay a security fix to perform a wholesale migration. A self-contained product may use a modular service with its own database and interfaces while still integrating oneSSO, oneSAAS and Kong. A content-free internal service may omit Strapi integration but cannot substitute Strapi for operational records in a content-heavy app.

The architecture team should publish working reference libraries and a seed app after the first pilot: Keycloak/BFF adapter, oneSAAS entitlement client, CMS adapter, token packages, OpenAPI generator config, GitLab pipeline and a small service template. Standards that lack reusable examples produce inconsistent implementations.
